Plain-language explanation: A plain-English guide to one project on tascperformance.com: adding written descriptions to the site's images. The companion sheet, "tasc-images-missing-alt-text", lists every image and the exact text to add. Read this first, then work through that list.

A short written description attached to an image, for example "Woman by the ocean in a white tasc bamboo T-shirt". Shoppers don't normally see it on the page. It is read out by screen readers, shown if an image fails to load, and read by Google and AI tools to understand what the image shows.

1) Shoppers who are blind or have low vision use screen readers, which read the page aloud. Without a description, an image is skipped or read as a meaningless file name. 2) Google Images and Google Search use the description to understand the picture, so good descriptions help tasc products show up. 3) AI shopping tools like ChatGPT and Google's AI answers read it too. 4) Accessibility is a legal consideration for US retailers (the ADA).

We checked every page on the site (995 pages). More than half of the images, 16,073 out of 29,923, have no description. That sounds huge, but it comes down to just 150 unique images. Most of them appear on every page (menu, footer and size guide) or in banners, so fixing each one once fixes it everywhere it appears.

Topic: What kinds of images are they?
Plain-language explanation: Mostly collection banners (the large photos at the top of collection pages), page banners, homepage tiles, feature photos on product landing pages, the size guide pictures, a few videos and the footer logo. Product photos in the main product galleries and collection grids already have descriptions. They are not part of this project.

Partly, and only as a patch. AudioEye (the accessibility tool on the site) fills in some missing descriptions after the page loads in a shopper's browser. Mostly it marks images as "decorative", which tells screen readers to skip them, and for a few it guesses a label, such as "TASC Logo". Search engines and some visitors may never see that patch, and a guess is not the same as a real description. Fixing it in the site itself is more reliable and doesn't depend on a third-party tool.

Topic: Why can't we just type descriptions into Shopify today?
Plain-language explanation: Shopify lets you save a description on any image (Content > Files > Alt text). But the parts of tasc's site design (the "theme") that show these banners currently ignore that saved description. So a developer needs to make a small, one-time change first. After that, anything typed into Shopify shows up on the site.

Topic: Step 1: Developer (one time, about 1 to 1.5 hours)
Plain-language explanation: Update two shared pieces of the theme ("lazypicture" and "responsive-image-wrapper") so they show each image's saved description. Also: write the size guide descriptions straight into the theme, mark the menu thumbnails as decorative, and update the top-banner video section. This is recommendation D2 on the recommendations page.

Go through the image list and paste the recommended text into Shopify for each image (instructions below). 131 images need text. Many banners come in a desktop and a mobile version with the same text, so there are only 92 different descriptions to enter. This can start before the developer is finished. Nothing is lost; the text simply appears on the site once step 1 is live.

After both steps, we re-scan the site to confirm the descriptions are showing. You can spot-check yourself: in Chrome, right-click an image, choose "Inspect", and look for alt="..." with your text in the highlighted line.

The rewards/discount app shows 2 small images of its own. tasc can't change those directly, so ask that app's support team to fix them. One blog post also has an empty image block that just needs deleting.

Section: How to use the image list
Plain-language explanation: "Image file" is the file name to search for in Shopify. "Number of pages" shows how many pages carry the image. "Page URL(s)" lists the full address of each page, one per line. For images that appear on every page, it says where on the site they sit instead (main menu, footer or size guide pop-up). "Recommended alt text" is the text to paste. "Target keyword" is the search phrase that page is aiming for, used where it fits naturally. "Plain description" is a simpler alternative if you prefer it. "Decorative?" is Yes for images that should stay blank. "Who does what" gives the steps in order. "Notes" adds context, such as whether it is the desktop or mobile version of a banner.

Section: How to use the image list
Plain-language explanation: Some images don't need a description, because they are background textures, small icons next to a label, or menu pictures sitting right beside text that already says the same thing. For these, the right answer is to leave the description empty on purpose, so screen readers skip them instead of repeating words. These rows say "(leave empty)". Don't type anything for them.

Section: How to use the image list
Plain-language explanation: Each one describes what is actually in the picture first. Where it reads naturally, it also includes the page's own keyword and the tasc brand or product name. Each is under 125 characters, which is about what screen readers handle comfortably. Fabric claims match what the page itself says: the Cloud Polo is beechwood, Sculptive is REPREVE recycled fabric, and the Motion Short is bamboo and cotton. Athletes are named from the Ambassadors page.

Section: How to use the image list
Plain-language explanation: Yes. These are suggestions. Keep them accurate to the picture, natural to read and under 125 characters. Avoid stuffing in extra keywords; Google treats that as spam and it sounds odd read aloud. Don't start with "Image of" or "Picture of", because screen readers already announce it's an image.

Section: How to enter it in Shopify
Plain-language explanation: 1) In Shopify admin, click Content, then Files. 2) In the search box, paste the file name from the "Image file" column. 3) Click the image to open it. 4) Paste the recommended text into the "Alt text" box. 5) Click Save. Repeat for the next row.

Section: How to enter it in Shopify
Plain-language explanation: 1) In Shopify admin, click Products and open the product named in the list. 2) In the Media section, click the video. 3) Choose "Add alt text". 4) Paste the recommended text and save.

Section: How to enter it in Shopify
Topic: For the ID.me logo (Community Discounts page)
Plain-language explanation: Same as most images: Content > Files, search "Untitled_design_1", paste "ID.me logo: tasc community discounts are verified through ID.me" and save. This one shows on the site straight away. It doesn't need the developer change.
Some suggested descriptions say "tasc" and others say "our" (e.g. "from our women's tops"). Pick one style and we'll make them all match.

Where the page doesn't name the exact product in a banner photo, the description uses general wording like "tasc tee" or "tasc hoodie" rather than guess. Someone who knows the product line can make these more specific.
Software that reads a web page aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.
The design template that controls how the Shopify store looks and how its pages are built.
A small, reusable piece of the theme. One snippet can draw dozens of images across the site, which is why fixing one fixes many.
An image that adds nothing a shopper would miss if they couldn't see it. It should have an intentionally empty description.
